Leila plays two games of chess.
The probability that she wins the first game is 0.6.
If she wins a game, the probability that she wins the next game is 0.7.
If she loses a game, the probability that she wins the next game is 0.4.
The tree diagram shows this information.

parts.t: Find the probability that Leila wins both games.
Find the probability that Leila wins exactly one of the two games.
Find the probability that Leila wins at least one of the two games.

sols: Exactly one win happens two ways: win then lose, or lose then win.
‘at least one’ is the complement of ‘none’

items.stem:
A bag contains n red balls and 4 blue balls.
Two balls are taken at random from the bag, without replacement.
The probability that both balls are red is 1⁄3.

parts.t: Show that n² − 5n − 6 = 0.
Solve the equation n² − 5n − 6 = 0 to find the number of red balls in the bag.
Find the probability that both balls are blue.

sols: There are n + 4 balls altogether, so P(first is red) = n⁄n + 4.
After a red ball is removed, n − 1 red balls remain out of n + 3, so P(second is red) = n − 1⁄n + 3.
collect all terms on one side
two numbers with product −6 and sum −5 are −6 and +1
A number of balls cannot be negative, so n = 6
The bag holds 6 red and 4 blue balls, 10 in total.
ms:
M1 for n⁄n + 4 × n − 1⁄n + 3 oe
M1 for 3n(n − 1) = (n + 4)(n + 3) oe
A1 for correct expansion and simplification to the given answer, nfww

M1 for (n − 6)(n + 1) oe, or correct use of the quadratic formula
A1
cao (−1 must be rejected)

items.stem:
Priya drops a drawing pin 200 times.
It lands ‘point up’ 130 times.

parts.t: Write down the relative frequency of the pin landing point up.

Estimate the number of times it lands point up.

Is she correct? Give a reason for your answer.

sols: Relative frequency = number of times point up⁄number of drops = 130⁄200 = 0.65
Estimated number = relative frequency × number of drops
Yes — the more times an experiment is repeated, the closer the relative frequency gets to the true probability, so a larger number of trials gives a better estimate.

items.stem:
Each day Kwame travels to work by car, by train or by bicycle.
On any day, the probability that he travels by car is 0.3 and the probability that he travels by train is 0.45.

parts.t: Find the probability that, on a particular day, Kwame travels by car or by train.
Find the probability that he travels by bicycle.

sols: Kwame uses only one method each day, so the events are mutually exclusive.
for mutually exclusive events, P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B)
Car, train and bicycle are the only possibilities, so the three probabilities add to 1.

List all the possible outcomes.
One has been done for you: HHT
Find the probability of obtaining exactly two heads.
Find the probability of obtaining at least one tail.

HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT

B1 for 6 or 7 correct, or 8 correct with one repeat

sols: P(not late on all three days) = 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.512
P(late at least once) = 1 − P(never late) = 1 − 0.512 = 0.488
The late day could be Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday — three different orders.

items.stem:
A box contains 10 batteries.
3 of the batteries are faulty and the rest work.
Two batteries are taken at random from the box, without replacement.

parts.t: Find the probability that neither battery is faulty.
Find the probability that at least one battery is faulty.

Three batteries are taken at random from the box, without replacement.
Find the probability that all three work.

sols: 7 of the 10 batteries work, so P(first works) = <sup>7</sup>⁄<sub>10</sub>.
Then 6 working batteries remain out of 9, so P(second works) = <sup>6</sup>⁄<sub>9</sub>.
P(at least one faulty) = 1 − P(neither faulty)
one fewer working battery and one fewer battery each time
